content: Balsam poplars, classified under Populus sect. Tacamahaca, are a group of approximately 10 species of poplar trees native to North America and eastern Asia. These trees are characterized by the balsamic scent of their buds, the whitish undersides of their leaves, and their rounded (non-flattened) leaf petioles in cross-section. They are large deciduous trees, typically reaching heights of 30 to 60 meters. Their leaves have a rounded base, a pointed apex, and a whitish waxy coating on the underside, which distinguishes them from most other poplar species. The name balsam poplar originates from the pleasant balsamic aroma emitted by their opening buds and leaves in spring. This scent is produced by a sticky resin on the buds, which also serves to protect them from insect damage. These trees are light-demanding and require significant moisture, but they are highly tolerant of very cold climates, growing further north than most other poplars, with the exception of aspens. The Ontario balsam poplar (Populus balsamifera, synonymously known as P. tacamahaca or P. candicans) is native to North America, thriving in alluvial bottomlands in the northeastern United States and Canada. It grows to a height of 30 meters and features yellow-grey bark that is thick and furrowed, with a blackish coloration at the base of the trunk. Its twigs are yellow-brown to brown, and its buds are coated with a layer of balsamic resin. The flowers and fruit of this species are similar to those of the white poplar. The western balsam poplar, also known as black cottonwood (Populus trichocarpa), is native to western North America, ranging from Alaska to northern California. It is the largest species of poplar, with recorded heights of up to 65 meters. This species holds significant importance in plant biology. In the mountainous regions of interior western North America, it is replaced by the willow-leaved poplar or narrowleaf cottonwood (Populus angustifolia). On September 15, 2006, it was announced in the journal Science that Populus trichocarpa became the first tree species to have its entire genome sequenced. Simon's poplar (Populus simonii), native to northwestern China, is often planted as a shade tree in northern European cities. It is an attractive ornamental tree with whitish bark and nearly rhombic leaves measuring 6–10 cm in length, which appear early in spring. Maximowicz's poplar (Populus maximowiczii), found in northeastern China, Japan, Korea, and eastern Siberia, is similar but has broader leaves. Another related species from Mongolia, the laurel-leaf poplar (Populus laurifolia), differs by having narrower leaves shaped like bay laurel leaves. Balsam poplars are primarily cultivated in parks for their ornamental value, light-colored bark, and pleasant springtime scent. The western balsam poplar is also planted as a timber crop. The wood of balsam poplars is soft, very lightweight yet strong for its weight, coarse, and fibrous. It does not polish or plane easily and is typically used for rough applications such as pallet boxes. Several hybrids between balsam poplars (particularly the western balsam poplar) and cottonwoods have been developed for wood production. These hybrids are selected for their exceptionally fast growth and disease resistance. Poplars are also of interest for biofuel production due to their rapid growth. Researchers are exploring genetic techniques to enhance their growth characteristics, such as increasing trunk girth and reducing canopy size, allowing more trees to be grown in smaller spaces. Additionally, efforts are being made to increase the proportion of cellulose relative to lignin in these trees, as this makes them easier to convert into sugars and ethanol for biofuel production.
